Q06.question: How do you prioritise competing tasks?
answers: I start each week by listing everything I need to do and marking each task by deadline and impact. Anything that affects customers or other teams goes first. Then I block time in my calendar for the bigger pieces so they don't get pushed aside by small requests. If two urgent things clash, I check with my manager rather than guess. In my last role this helped me keep a backlog of over forty tickets under control without missing any deadlines.

I use a simple rule: what is due soonest and what would cause the most trouble if it slipped. Each morning I pick my top three tasks and do the hardest one first while I have the most energy. I keep a running list for smaller jobs and batch them in the afternoon. When priorities change, I update the list straight away so I don't lose track. It sounds basic, but it keeps me calm on busy days.

In accounts, month end always brings competing deadlines. I keep a calendar of fixed dates like payroll and tax and plan everything else around them. I also tell people early if something will be late rather than waiting. For example, last quarter an audit request clashed with payroll, so I agreed a new date with the auditor in advance. Both were done properly, and nobody was surprised.

I look at who is waiting on each task. If someone else can't start until I finish, that usually comes first. Then I think about effort: quick tasks that unblock others are worth doing straight away. I check my list at lunchtime and again before I leave. In my retail management role, this approach helped me keep deliveries, rosters and customer issues moving at the same time.

I prioritise by deadline, but I also ask what the real deadline is. Sometimes a request marked urgent can wait a day, and sometimes a quiet request is actually blocking a big project. So I ask one or two quick questions before I decide. I use a shared task board so my team can see what I'm working on. That way people know when to expect things, and fewer requests come in twice.

In a busy clinic reception, priorities change by the minute. I always deal with the patient in front of me first, then phone calls, then emails and admin. I keep a notepad of follow-ups so nothing is forgotten after a rush. At the end of each day I go through the list and finish or hand over anything open. It helps that I'm organised by nature, and I like having a clear system.

I group tasks into must do today, should do this week, and could do later. I review the list with my manager once a week so we agree on what matters most. When something new comes in, I place it in one of the three groups before I start it. This stops me from jumping between jobs. In my last job, it helped me deliver three projects in the same quarter without working late every night.

I usually estimate how long each task will take and compare that with the time I have. If it doesn't fit, I decide what to delay or hand over before I start, not halfway through. I also protect a couple of hours each day for focused work. During a recent system upgrade I was also covering for a colleague, and this approach let me keep both on track.

For me, the first step is getting everything out of my head and onto one list. Then I sort it by urgency and importance and look for anything I can delegate. I'm honest when I can't take on more, and I suggest who else might help. In a warehouse role, this meant we kept the most urgent orders moving while longer jobs like stocktake still got done on schedule.

I start with anything that has a fixed external deadline, like a client delivery or a compliance report. Next come tasks that other people depend on. Internal improvements come last, but I still schedule them so they don't disappear. I check my plan at the start and end of each day. This has helped me become someone people can rely on to deliver what I promised.

Q07.question: Describe a time you worked in a team with a disagreement.
answers: On a project team, two colleagues disagreed about whether to build a new tool or buy one. The discussion kept going in circles. I suggested we list the costs, time and risks of each option side by side. Once it was on paper, it was clear that buying was cheaper and faster, and the colleague who wanted to build agreed. We also kept one of his ideas for a later phase, so he felt heard. The project went ahead on time.

In a café team, two staff kept arguing over who should clean up at closing. It was affecting the mood of the whole shift. I sat down with both of them and we made a closing checklist that split the jobs evenly by day. We stuck it on the wall. The arguments stopped, and closing became faster. Sometimes a disagreement is really about something being unclear.

During a university group project, one member wanted to change our topic halfway through. The rest of us were worried about time. I suggested a short vote after everyone had five minutes to make their case. We stayed with the original topic but added part of her idea as a section. She was happy with that, and we finished with a strong mark. Giving everyone a fair say mattered more than who was right.

At work, my manager and I disagreed about how to handle a slow supplier. He wanted to switch suppliers immediately, and I thought we should try fixing the issues first. I asked for two weeks to test a new ordering process. I tracked the results and shared them with him. Delivery times improved, so we stayed, which saved us the cost of changing. He appreciated that I backed up my view with data.

On a marketing team, the designer and the copywriter disagreed about how much text should go on a poster. I suggested we make two versions and show them to a small group of customers. The shorter version clearly did better, and both of them accepted the result. We now test small options like this before big campaigns. It turned an argument into an experiment.

In a nursing team, there was tension about how weekend shifts were shared out. Some people felt they always got the worst shifts. I offered to look at the last six months of rosters and shared the numbers at a team meeting. There was an imbalance, so we agreed on a rotating system. The tension eased quickly once people could see it was fair.

In an IT project, two developers disagreed about how to structure the database. I asked each of them to explain the main risk of the other's design. That helped them see each other's concerns, and they agreed on a mix of both. I wrote down the decision so we didn't revisit it later. The system has worked well since, and the two of them work together often now.

In a warehouse, a colleague and I disagreed about the best order to pick items. Instead of arguing, we each tried our method for a week and timed it. My method was faster for small orders, and his was faster for large ones, so we used both depending on the order size. It was a good lesson that both people can be partly right.

On a committee I was part of, members disagreed about how to spend a small budget. I suggested we set two or three goals first and then judge each idea against them. That moved the conversation away from personal preferences. We agreed on a plan in one meeting after weeks of debate. I like using shared goals to settle disagreements because it keeps things fair.

In my last role, a colleague felt I had taken credit for her work in a report. I was surprised, but I asked her to explain. She was right that her name wasn't on the analysis section. I apologised, corrected the report and made sure her work was mentioned to our manager. We've worked well together since. It reminded me to be careful about giving credit.

Q08.question: Tell me about a time you improved a process.
answers: Our team used to approve leave requests by email, and requests often got lost. I suggested a simple shared form that sent requests to the right manager and recorded the decision. I built it with a free tool we already had and tested it with one team first. Within a month every team was using it, and lost requests stopped completely. Managers also liked being able to see who was away at a glance.

At a bakery, we often ran out of popular items by midday. I started tracking sales by hour for a few weeks and used that to adjust the baking schedule. We baked smaller batches more often instead of one big batch in the morning. We sold out less often, and we also had less left over at closing. It was a simple change based on looking at the numbers.

In an office, new staff took nearly two weeks to get access to all the systems they needed. I listed every access request and found most could be requested before the person started. I made a checklist for managers to complete a week before the start date. New staff now have everything ready on their first day. It made a big difference to how welcome people feel.

In accounts payable, we checked every invoice by hand, even small ones. I suggested an automatic check for invoices under a certain amount that matched an approved order. Larger or unusual invoices still got a full review. This cut processing time by about a third and freed up time for the invoices that really needed attention. The auditors were happy with the controls too.

At a gym where I worked, members had to fill out paper forms for every class booking. I proposed moving bookings to the existing app, which already had a booking feature we weren't using. I set it up, trained the front desk staff, and put signs around the gym. Within two months most bookings were online, and the front desk had more time to help members on the floor.

In a hospital ward, handover between shifts often missed important details. I worked with two senior nurses to design a short handover template with the same headings for every patient. We trialled it for a month and asked staff for feedback, then made a few changes. Missed information dropped noticeably, and the ward manager rolled it out to two other wards.

In a logistics company, drivers called the office for every address change, which tied up the phones. I suggested sending address updates directly to the drivers' app. I worked with the IT team to test it on one route. Calls to the office dropped by more than half, and drivers spent less time waiting for answers. It was satisfying to fix something that frustrated everyone.

In my last role, our weekly sales report took a full day to prepare because it was built by copying data between spreadsheets. I learned some basic automation and set up a template that pulled the data in automatically. The report now takes about an hour. I wrote short instructions so others could run it while I was on leave. My manager used the saved time for more customer visits.

At a library, returned books were sorted by hand, which created a pile-up on busy days. I suggested sorting returns by section straight away using labelled trolleys, instead of one big pile. It sounds simple, but it cut reshelving time a lot, and books were back on the shelves the same day. Staff liked it because the work felt less chaotic.

In customer support, we answered the same five questions again and again. I collected the most common questions for a month, wrote clear answers and added them to our website and email templates. Repeat questions dropped, and our average reply time got faster. I also set up a monthly review so the answers stay up to date as products change.

Q09.question: Why are you interested in this role?
answers: I've spent the last three years working with data in a smaller company, and I'm ready for a role where analysis feeds directly into bigger decisions. This position combines reporting, problem solving and working with different teams, which are the parts of my current job I enjoy most. I also like that your company invests in training. I'd bring practical experience with spreadsheets and dashboards, and I'm keen to keep learning new tools here.

I've worked in customer-facing jobs for five years, and I really enjoy helping people solve problems. This role would let me use that experience while taking on more responsibility, like handling escalations and training new staff. I've also read about your focus on customer satisfaction, and that matches how I like to work. I think I could contribute from day one and grow with the team.

I'm interested because the role sits between operations and planning, and that's where I've done my best work. In my last job I improved stock planning and cut waste, and I'd like to do that on a larger scale. Your company is growing quickly, so there will be a lot to organise and improve. That kind of challenge motivates me.

I've just finished my degree in business, and I did my internship in a finance team. I enjoyed the mix of detail and problem solving. This graduate role offers rotations across different teams, which would help me find where I fit best. I'm reliable, I learn fast, and I'm happy to start with the basics and build up from there.

I've been in hospitality management for six years, and I'd like to move into a role with more planning and less night work. Many of the skills carry over: rostering, budgets, supplier relationships and handling problems quickly. This coordinator role uses those skills, and I think my background would bring a practical view to the team.

I like roles where I can see the result of my work, and this position does that. You'd be measuring success by how smoothly projects run and how happy clients are. In my current job I coordinate four or five projects at a time, so I'm comfortable juggling. I also like that the team is small, so I'd get to know everyone and contribute quickly.

I'm interested in this role because it focuses on improving processes, which is something I've done informally in every job I've had. I'd like to do it as my main responsibility. I've already worked with tools similar to the ones you use. I also value that your company supports flexible work, which would let me do my best work consistently.

I've worked in health administration for four years, and I'm interested in this role because it focuses on data quality. Good records make a real difference to patients and staff, and I've seen the problems poor data causes. I'm careful and organised, and I enjoy finding and fixing errors. I'd like to build my career in this area, and this role would be a great next step.

Honestly, the main reason is the type of work. You're looking for someone to manage client accounts from start to finish, and I enjoy building long-term relationships with clients. In my current role I manage around thirty accounts, and most have renewed every year. I'd like to bring that experience to a company with a bigger range of products.

I want to move into a role with a clear path to team leadership. I've been acting as a team lead for six months while my manager was on leave, and I enjoyed it. This position includes supervising a small team, which is exactly the experience I want to build. I also like your company's values around training and promoting from within.

Q10.question: Describe a time you learned a new skill quickly.
answers: When my team switched to a new accounting system, I had two weeks to learn it before month end. I went through the online training in the evenings, practised on test data, and made my own short notes. By the switchover I was confident enough to help two colleagues. Month end went smoothly, and my manager asked me to write a quick guide for future staff.

In a new job, I needed to learn basic SQL to pull reports. I did a free online course over a few weekends and practised by recreating reports we already had, so I could check my answers. Within a month I was writing my own queries, and I no longer had to wait for the IT team. It saved a lot of time and made me much more independent.

When I started at a florist, I had never made a wedding bouquet. The owner showed me once, and I practised with leftover flowers at the end of each day. I watched a few videos and asked for feedback each time. Within three weeks I made my first bouquet for a real customer, and she was very happy. I learn best by practising and asking for honest feedback.

When our office introduced a new project management tool, nobody had time to learn it properly. I spent a couple of lunch breaks exploring it, set up our team's board and showed everyone the basics in a fifteen-minute session. Within a week the team was using it daily. I enjoy picking up new tools and making them work for the people around me.

I took on a role where I needed to understand basic employment law for rostering. I read the relevant awards, took a short course, and asked our HR adviser to check my first few rosters. After a month I was doing them on my own with no errors. Being willing to ask for checking early helped me learn much faster.

At a warehouse, I needed a forklift licence within a month of starting. I booked the course straight away, practised during quieter shifts with a supervisor, and passed the assessment on the first try. It meant I could take on more tasks and cover for others when needed. I like learning practical skills that make me more useful to the team.

In a marketing role, I had to learn how to run online ads with no previous experience. I completed the platform's free certification, then started with a small budget and tracked the results every day. I adjusted the ads based on what worked. Within two months our cost per sign-up had dropped by about forty percent. Learning by testing small and adjusting worked really well.

When I moved into a lab assistant role, I had to learn several new testing procedures. I read each procedure carefully, watched a senior colleague do it, and then did it under supervision until I was signed off. I kept a notebook of tips and common mistakes. I was signed off on all the procedures within six weeks, which was faster than usual.

In my last job, I needed to learn basic budgeting for a small department. I asked our finance manager to walk me through last year's budget, then built a draft for the next year myself and had her review it. She only had a few changes. Now I manage the budget on my own and report on it each month. I'm not afraid to ask questions when I'm starting something new.

When our company started selling to customers overseas, I needed to learn how international shipping and customs paperwork worked. I read the carrier's guides, called their support line with questions, and made a checklist for each country we shipped to. Within a few weeks our international orders were going out without delays. The checklist is still used by the team.

Q11.question: Tell me about a time you used data to make a decision.
answers: We were deciding whether to extend our store's opening hours. Instead of guessing, I looked at hourly sales and foot traffic for three months. Late evenings were quiet, but early mornings had steady traffic before we opened. We opened an hour earlier instead of staying open later. Sales went up, and staff costs stayed about the same. The data pointed us in a different direction than we expected.

In a support team, we were debating whether to hire another person. I pulled ticket numbers and response times for the past year and found the busy periods were very seasonal. Instead of a full-time hire, we brought in a casual staff member for the three busiest months. Response times stayed on target, and we saved money. Looking at the pattern over time made the decision much easier.

At a gym, management wanted to cut a few classes. I looked at attendance data by class and time, and also at how many people tried a class once and never came back. Some quiet classes had very loyal members, so we kept those and cut two classes with consistently low numbers. Overall attendance didn't drop, and members were happy we didn't remove their favourites.

I was asked to choose between two suppliers for office supplies. I compared prices for our twenty most-ordered items, delivery times, and the number of errors in past orders. One supplier was slightly cheaper, but the other had far fewer errors. We chose the more reliable one because errors cost us time. Six months later, the decision still looked right.

In a hospital admin role, we wanted to reduce waiting times at the outpatient desk. I recorded arrival times and service times for two weeks. Most of the delay came from patients arriving at the same time for early appointments. We spread the appointment times out by ten minutes, and the average wait dropped by almost half. It was a small change backed by clear numbers.

For a newsletter, we had to decide which day to send it. I ran a simple test, sending it on different days for a month and tracking opens and clicks. Tuesday mornings clearly performed best, so we moved the send day. Engagement went up by about twenty percent. I liked that we didn't have to rely on opinions.

At a delivery company, we were considering a new route plan. I compared delivery times, fuel use and late deliveries for the old and new routes during a two-week trial. The new plan saved fuel but caused more late deliveries in one area. We kept the new plan for most areas and adjusted that one. Using the trial data helped us avoid making things worse.

In my last job, we were losing customers and nobody knew why. I looked at our cancellation records and found that most cancellations happened within thirty days of a price change notice. We started explaining price changes more clearly and offering a call with the account manager. Cancellations after price changes dropped noticeably. The data showed us where to focus.

At a school, we had to decide how to spend money on new books. I checked library borrowing records and found that some sections were borrowed far more than others, while some books hadn't moved in years. We spent more on the popular sections and removed old copies. Borrowing went up the next term. Students noticed the new books straight away.

In a café, we were thinking about adding a new lunch item. I looked at which items sold well and at what times, and saw a gap for something quick and cheap. We trialled a simple wrap for a month and tracked sales. It sold well and didn't take sales from other items, so we kept it on the menu. Testing first saved us from a risky change.

Q12.question: Tell me about a time you took initiative.
answers: I noticed our team kept paying for software licences for people who had left the company. Nobody had been asked to check this. I compared the licence list with the staff list and found fourteen unused licences. I raised it with my manager and helped cancel them, which saved a few thousand dollars a year. I also set up a monthly check so it doesn't happen again.

At my last job, our product shelves were often messy because restocking wasn't assigned to anyone. Without being asked, I made a simple restocking roster and suggested it at a team meeting. Everyone agreed, and the shelves stayed tidy after that. My manager mentioned it in my performance review, and I was given the chance to plan other store tasks.

I saw that new volunteers at our community centre didn't know where anything was. I wrote a short welcome guide with a map, key contacts and common tasks, and asked the coordinator if we could hand it out. It's now part of every volunteer's first day. Volunteers settle in faster, and the coordinator gets fewer of the same questions.

In an office job, I noticed we were printing hundreds of pages each week that people barely read. I suggested switching to digital copies for internal reports, and I set up a shared folder with clear names. Printing costs dropped, and people found the reports easier to search. It felt good to make a change nobody had asked for but everyone liked.

While working at a hotel, I noticed guests often asked the same questions about local transport. I put together a one-page guide with bus routes, taxi numbers and walking times, and placed it in every room. Guest questions at the front desk dropped, and several guests mentioned the guide in their reviews. It was a small effort that made a difference.

I saw that our team's shared drive was disorganised and people wasted time searching for files. I proposed a new folder structure, got agreement from the team, and spent a few quiet afternoons moving everything across. I also wrote simple naming rules. Finding files became much faster, and new staff picked up the system easily.

In a warehouse, I noticed some safety signs were missing or faded. I listed every sign that needed replacing, took photos and sent them to the site manager with a quote I had found. The signs were replaced within two weeks. I think safety is everyone's job, and it's better to raise these things early than after an accident.

At a clinic, I realised we had no backup plan if the booking system went down. I suggested printing the next day's appointments each afternoon and keeping them at reception. A few months later the system went down for half a day, and we kept running without any problems because of the printed list. The practice manager was very glad we had it.

In my last role, I noticed that many customer complaints were about one confusing line on our invoices. I drafted a clearer version and showed it to the billing team with examples of the complaints. They approved the change, and complaints about invoices dropped by more than half over the next two months.

I noticed our team wasn't tracking how long common tasks took, which made planning hard. I started a simple log for my own work and shared it as an example. A few colleagues joined in, and after a month we had enough data to plan our workload more accurately. Our manager now uses it to set realistic deadlines.
